newsitem.title: UK: British execs see need to develop brand identity.
newsitem.headline: British execs see need to develop brand identity.

text.p: British companies need to develop a modern British brand identify to sell their products both at home and abroad, one that builds on tradition without being a slave to the past, marketing executives said.

"We are trying to find the balance between tradition and the contemporary playground," Anthony Sell, chief executive of the British Tourist Authority (BTA), said on Tuesday at a the Walpole Committee seminar "The Competitive Edge of the British Brand."

The BTA, which works with the regional tourist boards of England, Wales and Scotland, is marketing Britain as a tourist destination by selling London as a modern, "cool" city along with the country's traditional lures of thatched cottages and beefeaters, Sell said.

Andrew Davies, managing director of Cricket, a communications, marketing, film and video production company, said companies need virtually to stand on their heads to get a fresh look at their products' key features in order to develop strong brand identities.
"Tradition is a major part of the equity of the British brand," Davies told the seminar. "But if we keep drawing it out we will be left with nothing but empty nostalgia," he said.

Davies said he objected to the current "Britain swings" image, fearing that like London's "swinging '60s" period it does not create a broad image that transcends time. "The problem is what's remembered is not the stuff of substance, it's the Carnaby Street and flares," Davies said. "It's not the breaking of shackles."
But by employing methods that force companies to look at themselves anew, "I'm suggesting a brand can tap into its British identify," Davies said.

While foreign luxury brands such as Hermes, Versace, Gucci and Chanel have successfully waged global marketing and advertising campaigns creating modern new images, their British counterparts are stuck in the past. "Britain ... has failed to break out of Edwardian imagery," Davies said.
Roger Putnam, sales and marketing director for Jaguar Cars Ltd, part of Ford Motor Co, noted that Jaguar's British identity "is a double-edged sword".

For too many consumers, Britain is not identified with the level of engineering, technology and style that a company like Jaguar is trying to sell. "While our costume dramas may sell like hotcakes abroad, Jane Austen doesn't sell cars," Putnam said.

David Aukin, head of film for Britain's Channel Four television network, said that for a long time the British public shunned British films. "There was almost a shame among British audiences about British films," he said. "You could only get over that if you said Americans love it, and they said, Oh, then we can love it."
One lesson the British film industry has learned is that successful films are made by aiming at a domestic audience, because the audience is understood, and then selling overseas.
"The success of the American film industry is built on its ability to serve its home audience and then (sell) abroad," Aukin said. "A film set in mid-Atlantic is a pudding of a film."
